articles.title: Norway faces backlash over 'deeply racist' proposal to jail citizens for West Bank business
articles.summary: Critics say Norway's proposed trade ban on Israeli settlements in Judea and Samaria effectively singles out Jews, calling the possible legislation racist.
articles.body: Critics are slamming Norway over new legislation that they say singles out Jews. The proposed law could send individuals to prison for up to three years for knowingly conducting certain forms of business with Israeli communities in the West Bank. The proposal, introduced by Norway’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, would prohibit the importation of goods originating in Israeli communities in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem and the exportation of goods to those communities. It would also restrict certain real estate transactions, construction and engineering services and investments in businesses headquartered and operating there. Intentional violations could result in fines, imprisonment for up to three years or both, while negligent violations could carry fines, imprisonment for up to six months or both, according to Section 7 of the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ official consultation document. ISRAEL’S E1 PLAN EXPLAINED: THE JERUSALEM-AREA CORRIDOR SPARKING INTERNATIONAL BACKLASH The measure remains under public consultation, with responses due Sept. 19, and has not yet been enacted. Israeli Ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon condemned the proposal in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Norway’s proposal to criminalize trade with Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria is the latest expression of their obsessive and openly hostile policy toward Israel. Instead of contributing to peace or regional stability, Norway has chosen political grandstanding, selective outrage and punitive measures against Israel," Danon said. "This approach damages bilateral relations, encourages rejectionism, and exposes just how detached Norwegian policy has become from the realities of the Middle East." The Israeli Foreign Ministry’s Northern Europe Department also referred Fox News Digital to a statement it posted on X condemning the proposal. US AMBASSADOR HUCKABEE SLAMS EXTREME GROUP OF ISRAELI SETTLERS FOR SEIZING PALESTINIAN HOMES ON WEST BANK "Norway’s legislative proposal to criminalize trade with Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria is the latest example of the Norwegian foreign minister’s obsessive anti-Israel activism on the global stage. Norway has repeatedly chosen to sacrifice its bilateral relationship with Israel in favor of one-sided rhetoric and hostile actions that serve domestic interests, undermine efforts to reach peaceful solutions, and are completely detached from the reality in the Middle East." In response to a request for comment from Fox News Digital, Norway’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs referred the outlet to its June 19 press release announcing the proposed legislation. The release states that Israeli settlements violate international law and undermine prospects for a two-state solution in which Israelis and Palestinians can live in peace and freedom. "By proposing legally binding prohibitions, the government makes it clear that Norwegian citizens and Norwegian companies must not profit from or support activities that help sustain Israel’s unlawful settlement activity in Palestine," Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said in the release. Eide also said the settlements contribute to "displacement, extreme violence and a situation that makes a peaceful solution impossible." UN AGENCY ACCUSED OF HAMAS TIES SEES ANOTHER EUROPEAN NATION CUT FUNDING The ministry cited United Nations Security Council findings and International Court of Justice advisory opinions supporting its position on the settlements’ illegality. It said the proposed restrictions would cover imports and exports, property purchases, certain property-related services and acquisitions of businesses with headquarters and production in the settlements, while safeguarding legitimate Palestinian activities and humanitarian assistance. The proposed legislation would exempt humanitarian activities, as well as transactions the government determines have "sufficient Palestinian ties" and do not contribute to the construction, expansion or maintenance of Israeli communities. Dag Juliussen, national director of the Norwegian branch of the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, said that the exemption could permit business with Palestinian residents while criminalizing comparable transactions involving Jewish residents in the same territory. "The bill is based on a fundamentally misguided understanding of the Middle East conflict, which in turn rests on a rewriting of history," Juliussen said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "In addition, such a law would effectively serve as a reward for terrorism and, at its core, is deeply racist toward Jews." CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND The consultation document does not characterize the proposal as targeting Jews. Instead, it says the measure is intended to prevent commercial activity that helps maintain Israeli communities beyond the pre-1967 lines, while shielding qualifying Palestinian commerce and humanitarian assistance. Under the proposal, exemptions would be evaluated according to the people involved who benefit from the transaction and whether the activity contributes to the construction, expansion or maintenance of an Israeli community. Juliussen said purchasing agricultural products from Muslim, Christian, Arab or Bedouin residents could be permitted, while purchasing similar products from Jewish residents could become a criminal offense. He argued that the determining factor would effectively be the identity of the seller. Norway formally recognized a Palestinian state in 2024 and has become one of Israel’s strongest European critics since the Hamas-led terrorist attacks of Oct. 7, 2023. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Juliussen warned that the proposed legislation would not bring Israelis and Palestinians closer to peace but could instead deepen divisions and encourage extremist forces in the region.

articles.title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges UVU knew of rooftop security risk before his assassination: legal filing
articles.summary: Charlie Kirk's family alleges Utah Valley University failed to secure rooftops and ignored warnings before the Turning Point USA founder's fatal shooting.
articles.body: Charlie Kirk's family has filed a notice of claim — a precursor to a lawsuit — against Utah Valley University, the state and key individuals involved in campus leadership and security decisions, alleging that their failures led to the Turning Point USA founder's wrongful death. "The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk’s close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," reads the filing, signed by Kirk family attorneys Loren Washburn, Brett Parkinson and Clifford Parkinson and dated Sept. 9. In one alleged exchange cited in the filing, Turning Point USA organizers told UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long that UVU students had informed them of rooftop access to the Sorenson Center, a building "pretty close" to where Kirk would be speaking the day he was killed — and directly west of the Losee Center, which is where his alleged killer fired the shot from. CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: TIMELINE OF UTAH CAMPUS SHOOTING, TYLER ROBINSON CHARGED "If this is true, it would be nice to either have it controlled access or allow one of my guys to be there as well," someone at TPUSA wrote to the chief, according to the filing. "If possible." "I got you covered," was Long's alleged reply. JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE IN WRITTEN ORDER Read the notice: Kirk, a 31-year-old father of two, was shot and killed on Sept. 10, 2025 in the campus courtyard, and authorities say a lone gunman took a sniper's perch on the Losee Center rooftop on the far side of the clearing. Lawyers for the suspect, 23-year-old Tyler Robinson, pleaded not guilty on his behalf at an arraignment nearly a year later. "His murder was entirely preventable and, in fact, would not have happened had the State of Utah and UVU followed through on their stated security promises, which included protecting the rooftops surrounding the quad where Charlie was speaking," said Brett Parkinson, counsel for the Kirk family. "Those failures not only robbed Charlie Kirk of his life, but also robbed his family of their husband, father, son, and brother, with impacts that will compound for the rest of their lives." The prospective plaintiffs in the filing are Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, and their two juvenile children. It also acknowledges potential claims from his parents, Robert and Kathryn. The filing does not specify monetary damages. In addition to the wrongful death claim, it also raises a claim of "state-created danger" under the U.S. Constitution. UVU said it is "aware of the notice of claim," and that it "addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes." "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community," the university said in a statement. REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR Kirk, who built TPUSA into the country's largest conservative campus and youth-oriented activist organization in the country, also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024. He had become a personal friend of the president's as well as other prominent figures, including leading Utah politicians, the notice continues. As a result, he had detractors, faced death threats, and publicly spoke about that before his assassination. articles.title: A Paris court awards Kim Kardashian 1 euro after her 2016 robbery
articles.summary: A Paris court awarded 1 euro to Kim Kardashian for having been the victim of an armed robbery in the French capital in 2016, the amount of compensation she had asked for, according to a lawyer involved in the case.
articles.body: SAINT-ETIENNE, France — A Paris court awarded 1 euro ($1.15) to Kim Kardashian on Tuesday for having been the victim of an armed robbery in the French capital in 2016, the amount of compensation she had asked for, according to a lawyer involved in the case. Kardashian has sought to move on since the court last year found eight people guilty for their roles in what the celebrity described as “the most terrifying experience of my life.” She and stylist Simone Harouche expressed gratitude to the French justice system in a joint statement. “The experience was deeply traumatic, and its impact has stayed with us. Today’s decision is not about the compensation, but about accountability and recognition,” the statement to The Associated Press read. “We are thankful to the Court and everyone who supported us throughout this process, and we hope to now move forward and continue to heal.” The court awarded a former receptionist at the Hôtel de Pourtalès 109,516 euros ($126,472), according to his lawyer. Kardashian had been staying at the hotel when the robbery gang targeted her. The receptionist said he had been traumatized by the Oct. 2, 2016, jewel heist during Fashion Week. He had sought 550,000 euros ($634,868) in damages and interest. His lawyer, Mohand Ouidja, welcomed the decision as a victory. The lawyer read the court’s written decisions pertaining to Kardashian and the others aloud to the AP. The court awarded the hotel 50,000 euros ($57,741). It awarded 1 euro — the amount she had requested — to Harouche, Kardashian’s stylist who was present during the robbery. French lawyers who acted for Kardashian during the trial didn’t respond to text messages and phone calls this week from the AP. Two of the robbers, dressed as police, forced their way into her suite, bound Kardashian with zip ties and tape and made off with more than $6 million in jewelry, including a diamond ring she’d worn that night to a Givenchy show. Because of their ages, the robbers became known in France as “les papys braqueurs,” or the grandpa robbers. Six of them were in their 60s and 70s when they were tried for armed robbery, kidnapping, gang association and other charges. With time already served in pretrial detention, none of those found guilty went back to prison. None of them appealed the verdict. Kardashian said in a statement issued after their conviction that she was “deeply grateful to the French authorities for pursuing justice in this case.” “The crime was the most terrifying experience of my life, leaving a lasting impact on me and my family,” the celebrity said. “While I’ll never forget what happened, I believe in the power of growth and accountability and pray for healing for all. I remain committed to advocating for justice and promoting a fair legal system.”

articles.title: ICC: Philippines' Rodrigo Duterte makes first in-person appearance at The Hague
articles.summary: He is due to be tried for crimes against humanity over thousands of deaths linked to his war on drugs.
articles.body:
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity.

He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs , which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily.

The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt on Wednesday, which marked the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago. He did not speak but waved at family members in the public gallery when proceedings ended.

Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and then skipped multiple hearings.

The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial .

The first trial date is scheduled for 30 November .

The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy.

The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, until 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC.

Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes recently told the court his client was suffering from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise.

Judges are deliberating whether Duterte is mentally fit to be tried and have ordered a medical assessment by three specialists.

That assessment has not been made public but according to AFP, defence lawyers say it shows Duterte thinks he is living in 2007 or 2008, that he is 84 or 85 years old, and was found to be unable to recall Donald Trump's name.

Relatives of those killed in Duterte's brutal anti-drugs campaign watched the proceedings over a livestream in Manila.

Llore Pasco, who lost two sons, told Reuters: "We're happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight."

Randy Delos Santos, who lost his teenage nephew in 2017, told AFP he was happy to see Duterte in court, adding: "We hope that his being physically fit will help speed up the hearings."

In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election.

Duterte's family is currently caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos.

The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025.

Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term.

But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial , where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office.

She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated.

articles.title: Olu Jacobs: Legendary Nollywood actor dies in Nigeria aged 84
articles.summary: Olu Jacobs was one of Nigeria's most recognised actors, whose career spanned several decades.
articles.body:
Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.

His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.

Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".

Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.

He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.

"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.

Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.

He later became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.

His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.

In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.

In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

articles.title: Former Indiana football star Sampson James spent 8 months homeless; then a grad student noticed his backpack in Austin, raised $17,000, and helped him get an apartment
articles.summary: US News: Sometimes, the smallest things lead to the biggest changes.In Sampson James’ case, it was a backpack.The former Indiana football star had been homeles.
articles.body: Sometimes, the smallest things lead to the biggest changes.In Sampson James’ case, it was a backpack.The former Indiana football star had been homeless for eight months. He lived on the streets of Austin and had little reason to be hopeful.Then, one afternoon, Jasper Steinmetz, a recent Indiana University graduate, walked past him and stopped. The red Indiana University athletic backpack was hard to miss. He had no idea that this homeless man was once a football star. They had a conversation that set off a chain of events and pulled James back from the edge.Within weeks, James received $17,000 in donations, a new apartment, and a second shot at a life that once seemed completely lost.A chance encounter that changed everythingJasper Steinmetz was walking along a path in Austin earlier this year. That’s when he spotted an unmistakable Indiana University athletic backpack. Steinmetz had recently graduated from IU himself. But the backpack was out of place. So, he decided to stop and ask the man carrying it about IU."I saw the Indiana University athletic backpack, and since I had just graduated from Indiana, we had that commonality. And I figured, you know, why not talk to him?" Jasper Steinmetz told CBS News.Former athlete on the streetsThe conversation revealed more than a shared college. Steinmetz learned that the homeless man was Sampson James. He had the same Hoosier roots, the same starting point. James shared that he had been homeless for eight months. After returning home, Steinmetz searched James’s name online. That’s when he learned just how far the fall had been.Sampson James had been a standout athlete, recruited as one of the best in his class. He discovered that James was a four-star recruit out of Avon High School in Indiana. He had the talent scouts wanted, the grades that impressed coaches, and the kind of future that small-town kids dream about.“He was an amazing athlete, really a standout star,” Steinmetz said.In 2019, he arrived at Indiana University as a freshman running back, exactly where he was supposed to be. But football can sometimes be unforgiving. He suffered a serious knee injury that derailed his athletic career. When James thought the worst was over, he got another diagnosis: bipolar disorder. The combination was too much. James left Indiana University in 2023 without finishing his degree. And all his football dreams vanished with it.He eventually lost everything, hit rock bottom, and was living on the streets of Austin. With almost no one left to turn to, he ended up on the streets. And the red backpack was the only possession left.How the backpack gave him a second lifeJasper Steinmetz noticed the backpack. He knew he had to help his fellow Hoosier. So he did. After meeting James, he set up a fundraiser online. The response was overwhelming. People wanted to help this man get his life back.The fundraiser raised $17,000 in donations. But Steinmetz had only begun. Leaving James homeless wasn’t an option. So he helped James secure an apartment."We just prepaid a bunch of rent and got him everything that he needed for the apartment," Steinmetz told the broadcaster.He wasn’t done yet. He wanted to make sure that James got all the support he needed to get back on track. So, Steinmetz joined James on that same trail again this week, this time looking at a brighter future."Now that all these people donated and you got the apartment, they really want to see you succeed," Steinmetz told James.James understood the weight of that expectation. He knew it came from a place of love. Strangers who genuinely cared about him."Oh yeah, and I'm big on not letting them down," James said.James is rebuilding his life now. He has a home. He has people rooting for him. For the first time in years, James isn’t just surviving. He’s allowed to want more. He has hopes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Kosovo's former president sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
articles.summary: Hashim Thaci has been jailed for crimes including torture and murder during Kosovo's independence war with Serbia.
articles.body:
The former president of Kosovo, Hashim Thaci, has been sentenced to 25 years in prison after being found guilty of war crimes.

A hearing at The Hague on Wednesday sentenced the 58-year-old for crimes during Kosovo's independence war against Serbia in the 1990s, in which more than 10,000 people died.

He was convicted after a three-year trial of crimes including murder, illegal arrests, torture and cruel treatment. A number of other allegations against him were not proven.

Thaci was a co-founder and commander of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), a group that fought for independence. He is regarded as a hero in Kosovo.

He was accused of killing nearly 100 people and of committing other atrocities including enforced disappearances.

Thaci was facing trial alongside three former commanders of the KLA who faced similar charges.

The Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) was set up in the early 1990s as a militant group of ethnic Albanians, in what was then a province of Serbia, and during the war is alleged to have carried out attacks on the region's ethnic Serb minority.

Thaci became Kosovo's first prime minister when it declared independence in 2008. He later became president but resigned in 2020 to face the charges in The Hague.

Thousands of people gathered in Kosovo to watch the verdict on large screens as they were handed down.

In the capital, Pristina, photographs and videos showed people in tears as they learned of the verdict.

articles.title: Seated exercises improving physical and mental wellbeing

articles.body:
People attending free seated exercises classes and laughing yoga said it has helped improve their physical and mental wellbeing.

Laugh, Move & Groove takes its sessions around community centres and care homes in Jersey to help keep people moving.

The not-for-profit group also works with charities as well to support people of different physical abilities to stay active.

It has been shortlisted for the BBC Radio Jersey Make a Difference Awards for its work.

Linda Crawford started coming to the classes in St Ouen's Parish Hall nine months ago.

She said: "I want to keep as fit as I possibly can... I thought it was sitting down so it wouldn't be very strenuous, but it is very strenuous.

"Because my body feels it's moved a lot, my mind feels calm as well.

"It's made an enormous difference for people on all kinds of levels, with all kinds of perhaps physical restrictions on how they can move."

Jackie Turner is one of the volunteers who helps lead the sessions.

She said: "It's just a fun environment and you can see that people enjoy it because it's a different way of exercising.

"It's also about the friendships and the social aspects as well because as you get older, sometimes the social aspects of your life fall away a little bit."

Col Samantha Shepherd has been on trial at Military Court Centre at Catterick Garrison in North Yorkshire, in connection with the handling of concerns raised by Gunner Jaysley Beck, from Cumbria.

The 19-year-old took her own life at Larkhill Camp in Wiltshire in 2021 after former Battery Sgt Michael Webber "pinned her down" and sexually assaulted her.

A board - which consisted of an Air Commodore, a Royal Navy captain and an Army colonel - returned a not guilty verdict for Shepherd, on the directions of a judge.

Assistant Judge Advocate General Edward Legard had told the board: "The Crown has concluded that there is insufficient evidence upon which you can safely convict Colonel Shepherd of the charge she faces."

Shepherd's barrister Derek Johashen said: "Colonel Shepherd is relieved by the decision.

Johashen said his client fully understood the impact on Gunner Beck's family.

He said: "Her thoughts remain with them, and always will.

"She always believed Gunner Beck, took her complaint seriously, listened to her and cared."

Shepherd has been in court alongside Maj James Hook, whose trial continues.

The two senior officers were accused of "conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline".

On Tuesday, the military court heard claims the 19-year-old had been "let down" when she told Shepherd and Hook "enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted" five months before she took her own life.

The board was told a chain of command failed to properly deal with the case.

Hook and Shepherd were charged by the Service Prosecution Authority over their handling of the case earlier this year.

The attack happened at a Royal Artillery adventure training exercise on Thorney Island, in Chichester Harbour, in July 2021.

At the time, Minister for Veterans and People, Louise Sandher-Jones MP described Jaysley's death as a "tragedy".

She said: "Let me be clear, there is no place for criminal or unacceptable behaviours within the military."

Assistant chief of general staff Maj Gen Jon Swift said the Army was "sorry we didn't listen to Jaysley when she first reported her assault".

He added: "We are determined to make sure the same mistakes don't happen again."

articles.title: NYC bodega cat Jabal returned after being snatched from street, owner had announced $500 no-questions-asked reward; woman in custody
articles.summary: US News: A three-month-old bodega cat has been reunited with his Brooklyn owner after he was allegedly snatched from a Park Slope street by a man and woman, tr.
articles.body: A three-month-old bodega cat has been reunited with his Brooklyn owner after he was allegedly snatched from a Park Slope street by a man and woman, triggering a neighborhood-wide search for the missing pet.Jabal, who had become a popular fixture at the 8th St. Mini Mart, was returned to his owner Imad “Jimmy” Innab on Tuesday after one of the alleged catnappers arranged for the kitten to be handed over to police. The woman is now in police custody, although she had not been charged as of Tuesday, according to the New York Post.The ordeal began last Thursday morning when Jabal slipped out of the store while Innab was opening up. Security footage showed a man and woman picking up the kitten around 7:18 am and walking away with him.Innab and his customers soon realized Jabal had not simply wandered off. The footage prompted neighbors to begin searching for him and putting up missing-cat posters around Park Slope.A customer later spotted the pair in Prospect Park and confronted them, telling them Jabal was not a stray but belonged to Innab. The couple fled, with the woman reportedly putting the cat inside a bag.According to the Post, the pair eventually took Jabal to Bushwick. As the search continued, Innab offered a $500 reward for his safe return and circulated photographs of the people believed to have taken him.The case took a turn Tuesday when the woman apparently decided Jabal needed to be returned. Rather than bringing him back herself, she reportedly sent her stepson to the 78th Precinct with the kitten.Police then brought Jabal back to the mini-mart, where Innab was waiting.'He knows I am the owner...I am his dad'“When he saw me, he just jumped! He knows that I am the owner of him. I am his dad,” Innab saidThe emotional reunion was particularly significant for the family because Jabal had joined the bodega only about a month earlier, following the death of Victoria, the family's previous cat. Victoria had lived at the store for 17 years before dying three months ago.Jabal had quickly become a neighborhood favorite, with regular customers getting used to seeing him around the store.Innab thanked the NYPD and the Park Slope community for helping bring his kitten home. He also urged people not to assume that an animal seen outside a shop or home is a stray.“Just leave it. Leave it for their home,” he said.As of Tuesday, police had the woman in custody, while the status of the man allegedly involved in taking Jabal was not immediately clear. articles.title: Poland: Russian drone found off Baltic coast had fragmentation warhead
articles.summary: A Russian drone recovered off Poland's Baltic coast earlier this week was fitted with an explosive device, a spokesman for the investigating prosecutor's off...
articles.body:
A Russian drone recovered off Poland's Baltic coast was found to be fitted with a fragmentation warhead and detonator, prompting concerns about potential security threats in the region.

The drone, identified as a Russian-made Gerbera-2, was separated from its warhead by Polish army special forces and defused on the beach before undergoing further examination at a military facility.

Poland is investigating a possible connection between this incident and a separate one in Lithuania, where a Russian combat drone entered Lithuanian airspace and was shot down after being found to also be equipped with explosives.

A Russian drone recovered off Poland's Baltic coast earlier this week was fitted with an explosive device, a spokesman for the investigating prosecutor's office told the PAP news agency on Wednesday.

The uncrewed aerial vehicle "contained a fragmentation warhead fitted with a detonator," the spokesman said in Poznań, Poland.

The drone was found on Monday near the seaside resort of Rusinowo in north-west Poland.

Army special forces separated the warhead from the drone and defused it on the beach, the spokesman said. It will now undergo further examination at a military facility.

According to prosecutors, the drone was a Russian-made Gerbera-2. Poland is also investigating whether there is a connection to a separate incident in neighbouring Lithuania.

On Tuesday night, a Russian combat drone entered Lithuanian airspace and was shot down. According to Lithuania's Defence Ministry, that drone was also fitted with explosives.

Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the drone found off Poland's Baltic coast may also have flown over Lithuania.

After attempts were made to neutralize it, the drone crossed the Lithuanian border into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and then most likely flew over the Baltic Sea.

Both countries were jointly investigating the incidents, he said.

Poland, an EU and NATO member, is a key political and military ally of Ukraine, which has been defending itself from Russia's full-scale invasion.

At the same time, Warsaw considers Moscow a security threat. A Russian drone strike on a train travelling from Kiev to Warsaw just before the Polish border alarmed the Polish government as recently as Sunday.

articles.title: What is BRICS Pay, and can it rival the West’s SWIFT payments system?
articles.summary: BRICS Pay is a decentralised digital system for making international payments in currencies other than the dollar.
articles.body:
The central theme of the BRICS bloc of nations is to push back against the global economic dominance of Western countries. That core value was very much at the centre of this year’s 18th BRICS Summit , which took place last week in India.

At the September 12 and 13 summit in New Delhi, leaders committed to expanding local currency trading systems and cross-border payment systems by investing in BRICS Pay, an initiative of the BRICS Business Council.

“We acknowledge the work done to study the cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels, and the discussions on promoting trade settlements and investments using BRICS local currencies, while respecting national priorities and acknowledging that there is no one-size-fits-all approach,” leaders said in a joint declaration as the summit concluded.

They also encouraged the BRICS Payments Task Force (BPTF), a collaborative central bank expert platform focused on cross-border payment mechanisms, to “facilitate practical solutions for cross-border payments among BRICS countries, which are fast, low-cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent and safe”.

Manoj Kewalramani, chairperson of Bengaluru-based think tank Takshashila Institution’s Geostrategy Programme, told Al Jazeera that the declaration indicates “that the quest is not for a single system, but perhaps a suite of options that can be agreed between member states to de-risk their trade and financial dealings”.

While the New Delhi declaration did not indicate that BRICS nations aim to replace the dollar or build their own common currency, it highlights how BRICS is increasingly trying to find alternate payment systems amid geopolitical tensions and Western trade sanctions on members of the bloc, Russia and China.

If systems like BRICS Pay become fully operational, they could work as alternatives to Western payment systems like SWIFT, however.

Proposed by the BRICS Business Council in 2018, BRICS Pay is a decentralised digital payment ecosystem developed to simplify payments between BRICS countries.

BRICS stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, the initial members of the informal trading group. It was founded in 2006, with South Africa joining in 2010. Since then, more countries have joined – Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia.

In all, that’s 11 member countries, accounting for roughly 49 percent of the world’s population and about 40 percent of the world’s gross domestic product (GDP).

According to the BRICS Pay website, it is a “strategic infrastructure” which can also be used by “friendly states” of BRICS countries. It is also meant to offer a “compatible option” for Western payment systems like SWIFT, Visa and Mastercard, but does not intend to replace them.

The payment system was officially endorsed by the BRICS Business Council in 2024 and in August this year, before the BRICS summit in New Delhi, the group’s finance ministers and central bank officials met in Jaipur, India, to discuss advancing the project.

It is currently in pilot and phased rollout stages and is not yet globally operational for all members.

BRICS Pay will connect national payment systems of member countries to each other so international payments can be made more easily.

This will mean that trading transactions between entities or individuals in two different countries can be processed in local currencies, removing the involvement of other currencies such as the dollar.

Payments in local currencies will be settled using QR codes, digital wallets or mobile applications.

Andrey Mikhaylishin, the CEO of BRICS Pay, told India’s Asian News International (ANI) on September 12 that many countries want to use their own payment infrastructure in this way.

“For example, Russia has Mir and a Fast Payment System. India has RuPay and UPI. Furthermore, the European Union is building its own payment infrastructure, called the European Payments Initiative. The UK also wants to create and build its own infrastructure,” he noted, adding that these systems, however, do not automatically work with each other.

“BRICS Pay is a payment ecosystem that can connect national payment infrastructures and give people the ability to use them when they are travelling in countries, not only within BRICS but around the world. It’s helpful for tourists who come to the country and gives them the service of using their own domestic means of payment,” he explained.

“On the other hand, we can talk about companies and banks that need to make settlements with each other. We do that too for B2B (Business-to-business) settlements. It’s a new kind of architecture, a fully decentralised architecture for settlements between countries,” he said.

“We don’t speak about de-dollarisation,” he said.

“We give more flexibility and more types of payment options for our citizens, companies and banks. If they want to use the dollar, they can use the dollar, too,” he added.

How are international payments made currently?

While BRICS Pay has yet to become fully operational, most transactions between countries, companies and even tourists take place through Western cross-border payments like SWIFT.

SWIFT is a cooperative company under Belgian law. It is owned by up to 3,500 shareholders linked to approximately 11,000 financial institutions across the world.

The system is overseen by the G10 central banks, as well as the European Central Bank, with its lead overseer being the National Bank of Belgium.

SWIFT is essentially a network used by banks to send secure messages about transfers of money and other transactions.

So if a company in India wants to pay a company in Europe, the payment currently passes through SWIFT.

More than 11,000 financial institutions around the world use SWIFT, making it the backbone of the international financial transfer system.

While most payments are made in the US dollar, the system also includes payments in the British pound, Indian rupees, euros, and yen, among others.

However, Russia has been banned from using the system due to its war on Ukraine. In February 2022, just days after Moscow’s invasion of Kyiv began, Western nations moved to block certain Russian banks’ access to the SWIFT international payment system.

This has made it harder for Russian banks to communicate with peers internationally, even in friendly countries such as China, slowing trade and making transactions costlier.

Since 2024, at the annual BRICS Summits, Russia has been pushing for alternative payment systems and promoting national currencies, in an effort to bypass Western sanctions.

Alejandro Reyes, adjunct professor in the department of politics and public administration at the University of Hong Kong, said that in such situations, BRICS Pay’s attractiveness is obvious.

“Russia’s experience with sanctions and the broader concerns among many emerging economies about dependence on Western-controlled financial infrastructure have created demand for alternatives,” he said.

But he stressed that BRICS is not a homogeneous bloc.

“India, Brazil, China, Russia the UAE and the other members have very different relationships with the dollar, with Western financial institutions and with one another. They also have different regulatory systems, capital controls and strategic interests,” he said.

“So the more plausible model is not a single centralised ‘BRICS payment system’, but a network of interoperable national systems, connecting mechanisms such as India’s UPI, Brazil’s Pix and other domestic payment platforms and allowing more transactions to be settled in national currencies.”

BRICS Pay has been designed to provide a parallel, interoperable channel to the Western SWIFT network and analysts say it has not been designed to replace it.

“I don’t see BRICS Pay replacing SWIFT globally in the foreseeable future. SWIFT has enormous advantages of scale, trust, standardisation, compliance infrastructure and network effects built up over decades,” Reyes said.

“But that doesn’t mean BRICS Pay is insignificant. If it develops successfully, it could gradually reduce reliance on SWIFT in particular trade corridors, especially for intra-BRICS transactions conducted in local currencies,” he explained.

“In that sense, the real challenge to SWIFT may be less that one new system displaces it and more that the international payments architecture becomes more plural and fragmented, with several networks operating alongside one another,” he added.

Have BRICS countries been using other payment systems?

Yes. BRICS countries have been using domestic payment systems.

UPI (or Unified Payments Interface) is largely used in India for retail transactions. While it is also present in other countries, including Singapore, France and the UAE, UPI is not used heavily for international trade, according to Kewalramani.

Brazil has also been using a payment system called Pix, which enables people to settle transactions through their bank accounts, while China uses Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS).

Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for the Asia Pacific at Natixis in Hong Kong, told Al Jazeera that CIPS already avoids the SWIFT system.

But she stressed that while these domestic systems within BRICS countries exist, “the key question here is whether they can be linked” through systems like BRICS Pay.

articles.title: Trump brings new heat to controversial UN agency as alleged Hamas ties engulf scores of employees
articles.summary: UN Watch says UNRWA completed at most 13 of 50 reforms, accusing the agency of counting draft policies and pilot programs as finished overhauls.
articles.body: President Donald Trump recently amplified a report about a U.S. government investigation that referred more than 100 current or former UNRWA employees over alleged ties to Hamas — as a new watchdog report accuses the UN agency of overstating how much it has reformed. The scrutiny, which included Trump sharing the report on Truth Social in August, comes as Geneva-based UN Watch released a report Monday challenging UNRWA’s claim that it has completed 41 of the 50 reforms recommended by an independent review led by former French Foreign Minister Catherine Colonna. UN Watch says that when it compared UNRWA’s claims with what Colonna actually recommended, at most 13 of the 50 reforms had been completed as prescribed. The group argues that UNRWA repeatedly counted drafting policies, launching pilot programs or creating plans as completed reforms even when full implementation had not occurred. UN AGENCY ACCUSED OF HAMAS TIES SEES ANOTHER EUROPEAN NATION CUT FUNDING "UNRWA is grading its own homework—and giving itself credit for reforms that exist mainly on paper," UN Watch Executive Director Hillel Neuer told Fox News Digital. "A policy is not a reform if it is ignored, unenforced or blocked by staff unions dominated by Hamas." Among the examples cited in the report is staff vetting. UNRWA lists a "Commercial Vetting Pilot & Costed Plan" as completed, along with other screening measures. UN Watch argues that a pilot and implementation plan do not amount to a fully operational outside vetting system. The report also challenges UNRWA’s education reforms. UNRWA lists systematic textbook reviews and randomized classroom inspections among completed steps, while a policy prohibiting problematic educational content is still described as "in progress." Colonna herself said when presenting her review in April 2024 that some educational content remained problematic, citing "glorification of jihad," incitement to violence and maps that did not show Israel, while calling for a zero-tolerance approach. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS MORE THAN $1B IN UN BUDGET CUTS AS REFORM PUSH GAINS MOMENTUM Pressed by Fox News Digital at Tuesday’s UN briefing over who independently verifies whether the reforms are actually working on the ground, UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric defended the process. "It is not just checking boxes for the sake of checking boxes," Dujarric said, "It’s about the implementation of those things." Dujarric said UNRWA regularly reports to the General Assembly, holds integrity meetings open to member states and gives governments opportunities to scrutinize what the agency is doing. WATCHDOG DEMANDS APOLOGY AFTER UN MEMORIAL ERRONEOUSLY HONORS HAMAS TERRORIST Asked specifically about staff screening, he said UNRWA relies in part on countries where it operates. "We rely on the member states also, where we operate, who have the capacity to check people to do so," Dujarric said, adding that UNRWA shares staff lists with Israeli, Jordanian, Lebanese and Syrian authorities. "If there are concerns, they need to be shared directly with UNRWA. When they are, they take action." The Colonna review was commissioned by UN Secretary-General António Guterres in February 2024 after allegations that UNRWA employees had participated in the Oct. 7 attacks. Guterres accepted all 50 recommendations in April 2024 and agreed with UNRWA leadership to establish an action plan to implement them. articles.title: Photos: Gaza building collapse kills 20, including women and children
articles.summary: Israel-hit building collapsed in Gaza City, killing 20 and leaving dozens trapped under the rubble.
articles.body:
At least 20 people, including women and children, have been killed and dozens more are feared trapped under the rubble after a Gaza apartment building collapsed following damage sustained in earlier Israeli attacks, authorities in the Palestinian enclave have said.

The six-storey building, which had four apartments on each floor, crumbled on Wednesday onto nearby homes and tents in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, according to the Civil Defence.

Mahmoud Basal, a spokesperson for the agency, told Al Jazeera, “Civil Defence teams are still working to recover martyrs from under the rubble and search for missing people. Until now, there are nearly 100 Palestinians still under the rubble of this building.”

Local media reported that the building had previously been hit by Israeli strikes, leaving it cracked and structurally unsound before it collapsed.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has destroyed or damaged thousands of buildings across the besieged territory, and Israel has severely restricted the entry of construction materials needed for repairs.

With so many Palestinians left homeless and severe shortages of construction materials, many displaced families have been forced to return to homes damaged by Israeli bombardment.

articles.title: China willing to ‘safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights’, official says
articles.summary: China says the US-Israel war on Iran highlights flaws in the Middle East’s ‘existing security architecture’.
articles.body:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Beijing is “willing to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with Iran, and safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights and interests”.

The foreign ministers met in Beijing on Wednesday, a week before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the United States, where he is set to meet his US counterpart, Donald Trump, and they are expected to discuss the war on Iran and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.

“We encourage Iran and the US to stay rational and restrained,” Wang said.

“We urge all parties to take effective measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at an early date,” he said, adding that China “does not want to see regional tensions to spill over further into Yemen and the Red Sea”.

He also told Araghchi that Tehran and Washington should “rebuild the negotiation mechanism based on the consensus reached so far”.

“The current situation once again demonstrates that the existing security architecture in the Middle East is inadequate and needs to be reformed and strengthened,” Wang said.

China stands ready to promote peace, fairness and justice in the region, and its policy towards Iran has remained consistent and stable, he added.

Earlier this week, Beijing refuted US media reports that Chinese entities supplied Tehran with satellite images of a military base housing US troops in Jordan, and Trump said in April that he wrote to Xi a letter “asking him” not to sell weapons to Iran.

China is a top economic partner of Iran and the largest buyer of Iranian crude oil.

articles.title: EU chief von der Leyen proposes ‘associate member’ status for Canada
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week that Canada was seeking a ‘unique alliance’ with the European Union.
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has raised the prospect of Canada becoming the 27-nation European Union’s first “associate member”, a striking overture as both seek to pivot away from a hostile United States under President Donald Trump.

Von der Leyen’s statement on Wednesday came after Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week that Canada was seeking a “unique alliance” with the EU, but not membership.

Von der Leyen told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that, as democracies are facing a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together.

“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told Carney, who was attending her annual keynote speech.

The first foreign head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” address, his visit comes in advance of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month. Carney will deliver his own address to the European Parliament on Thursday.

Von der Leyen said it was time to move from cooperation based on a trading relationship to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible”.

She said that the EU and Canada would work together on sectors ranging from manufacturing to AI, critical minerals and energy.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she added.

EU treaties do not envision the possibility of becoming an “associate member”. But the idea was first proposed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz this year regarding Ukraine.

Under the plan, which met a cold reception in Kyiv as it pushes for full membership status , Ukraine would have been allowed to attend the bloc’s summits and have a representative in the European Commission.

It would have also benefitted from parts of the EU budget, but without full voting rights.

Buffeted by US tariffs and competition from China, Brussels and Ottawa already enjoy considerable cooperation.

A free-trade agreement (CETA) that abolished almost all tariffs has been credited with boosting trade in goods and services by more than 80 percent since 2016.

Furthermore, Canada became the first non-EU country to join a flagship defence loan programme this year.

“We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest – but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work,” von der Leyen said. “So, we are joining forces voluntarily.”

articles.body: A month ago, Pakistan was celebrating. Its leaders, Shehbaz Sharif and Asim Munir, posed for cameras in Mecca, ink still wet on a defence pact that promised to bind the fate of Islamabad to that of Riyadh and Ankara.A month later, the pact is facing perhaps its most uncomfortable test yet.Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that it had intercepted a Houthi drone heading towards Mecca, calling the security of Islam's holiest city a 'red line'. The Houthis flatly denied targeting Mecca and, in the same round of escalation, claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Yemen's Marib province, a claim Riyadh has not confirmed.The message behind the pact was simple and stirring, an attack on one is an attack on all. Today, as Saudi Arabia and the Houthis trade accusations and the conflict moves deeper into Saudi territory and Yemen, Pakistan is discovering that grand declarations are far easier to sign than to honour.Pakistan is now walking a tightrope between backing Saudi Arabia and avoiding a confrontation with Iran.How it gets off that rope, and whether it can do so without falling, may say more about the limits of 'solidarity' than any communique ever could.A pact born in euphoria?When Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed their joint defence agreement in Mecca last month, it was billed as a landmark moment, a triangle of Sunni Muslim power standing shoulder to shoulder against outside threats.Pakistani officials spoke of it with unmistakable pride, and defence minister Khawaja Asif was quick to declare that the pact would kick in the moment Saudi Arabia faced an unprovoked attack or spillover from the war in Yemen. There should be no doubt about it, he insisted.That confidence looked reasonable enough at the time. The region was tense but the front lines in Yemen had been largely frozen since 2025 Gaza agreement, and the bigger drama was unfolding around the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran and the United States were locked in their own confrontation. Pakistan could afford to sound bold because the pact's first real test seemed a distant hypothetical.Enter the HouthisA month later, that hypothetical arrived far earlier than expected as Iran-backed Houthi fighters broke out of their static positions and surged towards the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, seizing the port city of Mokha and a string of Red Sea islands from Saudi-backed Yemeni forces.Almost simultaneously, a drone strike hit Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline, the artery that carries a significant share of the kingdom's oil away from the reach of Hormuz. With that pipeline hit and the Houthis tightening their grip on the coast, Saudi Arabia suddenly found both of its alternative export routes under pressure.For Riyadh, this was precisely the kind of scenario the Mecca pact was meant to guard against. Attacks were reaching Saudi territory, while the fighting in Yemen was again threatening to spill into a wider regional confrontation.Mecca under threatThe pressure on the pact became even harder to ignore when Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted a Houthi drone heading towards Mecca and called the security of Islam's holiest city a 'red line'.The Houthis rejected the Saudi account, denying that they had targeted Mecca. In the same round of escalation, they also claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Yemen's Marib province, a claim Riyadh has not confirmed.That puts Pakistan in an awkward position. Saudi Arabia is not just a close partner but one of the three signatories of the Mecca pact. Iran, meanwhile, remains central to the Houthi question and is a neighbour Islamabad cannot afford to alienate.Pakistan has condemned the attacks, but its response has remained cautious. At the UN, its ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad said the escalation had brought the conflict to an 'extremely dangerous juncture', while stressing the need for de-escalation and regional stability.That caution was also reflected in remarks by Pakistan's military spokesperson, who described the pact as an arrangement for 'collective deterrence' with no 'regional aspirations'.Turkey and Pakistan have also said the agreement has not yet been formally ratified, raising questions over when it would actually take effect and what would trigger it.For a pact announced with such fanfare, those questions have surfaced far sooner than expected.Why Iran complicates everythingSo why is Pakistan being so cautious? The heart of Pakistan's dilemma is Iran.Unlike Turkey, which sits at some remove from the Gulf's sectarian and strategic fault lines, Pakistan shares a long, porous border with Iran and has spent years carefully managing that relationship. Tehran is not merely a bystander in this crisis, it is the patron whose support has allowed the Houthis to become the sophisticated fighting force now humbling Saudi Arabia's defences.Pakistan has also been quietly trying to mediate between Washington and Tehran over their wider confrontation, a role that would collapse overnight if Islamabad suddenly deployed forces against an Iranian-backed militia.That balancing act explains the studied vagueness coming out of Islamabad. Condemning drone strikes on Saudi soil costs Pakistan nothing, and it duly issued a statement calling the pipeline attack a violation of international law and Saudi sovereignty. But translating that condemnation into military commitment under the Mecca pact would mean picking a side in a conflict that has Iran's fingerprints all over it, at the exact moment Pakistan is trying to keep lines open to Tehran.Turkey has taken a similarly cautious line, praising Saudi restraint rather than promising action of its own.US absence makes the rope narrowerPakistan's caution is not happening in a vacuum. The United States, Saudi Arabia's traditional security partner, has shown little appetite to intervene either.Reports suggest Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman dialled US President Donald Trump twice asking for American military action against the Houthis, and was twice turned down. Trump has instead spoken of direct contacts between his administration and the Houthis themselves, a move one Yemen expert warned only hands the rebels the legitimacy and global attention they crave.If Washington, with all its firepower and decades-old ties with Riyadh, is reluctant to get drawn into this fight, it becomes far easier to understand why Islamabad, with a fraction of that capability and a shared border with Iran, is equally hesitant.Pakistan cannot be expected to charge in where the United States itself is reluctant to go. Yet that hesitation still sits awkwardly with the confident language used when the pact was signed.A toothless tiger?None of this means the Mecca pact is dead. Its defenders would argue that treaties of this kind are rarely triggered at the first sign of trouble, and that quiet diplomacy, such as Pakistan's warning to Iran, counts as a form of support.Saudi Arabia itself has other tools available, from its well-funded air force to potential quiet assistance from Israel, and may not need Pakistani boots on the ground to deal with the Houthi threat.ALSO READ | From Mecca's red line to the 'Gate of Tears': How US-Iran war is closing in on MBSBut perception matters in geopolitics almost as much as capability, and right now the perception is damaging. A pact unveiled with talk of collective defence has, within a month of its signing, produced statements about rules not yet being discussed and an agreement not yet formally ratified, precisely when its central member is under direct attack.Whether or not Pakistan ever intended to send troops to the Red Sea, the hesitation has already raised questions over what the pact actually requires its members to do when one of them comes under attack.For Pakistan, that may now be the real test of the Mecca pact: not what it promised on paper, but how far Islamabad is prepared to go when those promises become difficult to keep.ALSO READ |'Special significance to Muslims': India condemns Houthi drone attack near Saudi Arabia's MeccaCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sussex Wildlife Trust wants Brighton Marina silt disposed offshore
articles.summary: Brighton Marina wants to restart dredging next year but still needs a site to dispose of the silt.
articles.body:
A wildlife trust has called for a new offshore disposal site to be found for sediment dredged from Brighton Marina, saying it remains concerned about plans being explored off Newhaven.

Brighton Marina has been looking for a long-term disposal site since Sussex Wildlife Trust successfully challenged a licence in 2025 for disposal of sediment at Rottingdean.

The marina has said dredging is needed to maintain safe access and there are limited options available for disposal sites.

Sussex Wildlife Trust said Newhaven was a "protected area" that sat adjacent to the Beachy Head West Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ).

Campaigners previously claimed the silt was a " black, thick, slimy, petrochemically smelling sludge ", but Premier Marinas, which owns Brighton Marina, said dredged silt was regularly sampled to confirm it was not harmful.

John Cervenka, Premier Marinas chief operating officer, said: "Maintaining safe navigational access to Brighton Marina is not optional. It is a legal requirement and fundamental to the operation of the marina."

He said the marina was a major centre of economic activity.

According to the marina, about 150 businesses depend on the site, creating jobs for about 1,200 people, with more than eight million visits each year.

Premier Marinas said Newhaven had been identified as a potential alternative by Sussex Wildlife Trust.

However, the trust said in a statement on social media : "We have not promoted or endorsed Newhaven over any other option."

The trust said: "Newhaven sits adjacent to Beachy Head West MCZ, and we remain concerned about potential impacts on this protected area.

"Our preferred option is a new offshore disposal site, well away from the MCZ."

The trust said that Newhaven was already used for dredge disposal by Newhaven Port, and there was currently no available data on the impacts of additional disposal there.

Until it saw further evidence, it did not have a view on whether Newhaven was suitable, it added.

"We will respond to any future licence application based on the ecological evidence it contains," it said.

Brighton Marina hopes to submit a marine licence application to the Marine Management Organisation in November.

If approved, maintenance dredging could restart next spring.

articles.title: Norway’s sovereign wealth fund profits from Israeli holdings amid genocide
articles.summary: As Gaza is being destroyed, the so-called oil fund enjoys robust returns from companies linked to Israel’s military.
articles.body:
The value of Norway’s sovereign wealth fund’s investments in Israeli companies has increased, prompting ethical concerns among campaign groups and charities as the war in Gaza continues.

The fund, the world’s largest, cut its Israeli holdings from 61 to 29 companies last year, citing “the serious humanitarian crisis” in Gaza.

Although it has made no new investments in Israeli firms since, returns from its remaining holdings reached $2.4bn in the first half of 2026 – a rise of 15.7 percent since the end of 2025.

The fund “represents enormous economic and political power”, Rami Samandar, head of Norway’s Palestine Committee, told Al Jazeera. “When Norwegian public capital is invested in companies whose activities contribute to Israel’s military aggression, the occupation and the infrastructure that sustains it, are very problematic and should be stopped.”

Launched in the 1990s to manage profits from oil and gas companies, the so-called “oil fund” is managed by Norges Bank.

“We believe that Norway, through the Norwegian oil fund’s investments, is failing to comply with its obligations under international law and is contributing to the maintenance of Israel’s occupation and oppression of the Palestinian people,” Samandar said.

The value held in the Israeli drone-camera company NextVision Stabilized Systems has increased to $25.9m from $21m in 2025 over the period. The state-owned Israel Aerospace Industries, Israel’s largest aerospace and defence company which supplies the military, buys equipment from NextVision.

The fund also profits from stakes in One Software Technologies, which, according to Who Profits, a group that researches companies involved in Israel’s occupation, provides the Israeli Civil Administration maintenance services for the biometric identification system deployed at checkpoints in the occupied West Bank. Formula Systems, another company, provides software services to the Israeli military through its subsidiary TSG.

Mads Harlem, an international lawyer at Save the Children Norway, told Al Jazeera that the fund should divest from NextVision so long as it “has not implemented adequate measures to prevent its products from contributing to violations of international humanitarian law”.

A spokesperson for Norges Bank Investment Management said the fund’s ethical framework is under review.

The finance ministry has “adopted temporary ethical guidelines and changes to the management mandate that apply until a new framework is in place. During this period, Norges Bank shall not decide on observation or exclusion of companies,” the spokesperson said. “The fund is broadly invested in line with the mandate we have been given by the ministry of finance,” they continued, adding that the ministry “sets a benchmark index that determines which markets and companies the fund is to be invested in, and the Israeli market is part of that index.”

The review is expected to conclude by October 15.

“In our view, this [period] leaves Norway unable to fully meet its obligation to prevent serious violations of international law,” said Harlem.

Pal Nygaard, professor at BI Norwegian Business School and a member of Historians for Palestine, a group which examines the companies in question, was disappointed to see the fund’s continued investments in NextVision.

“They didn’t sell the stocks when it’s thoroughly documented that the company is contributing to Israel’s war crimes,” he said. “The most reasonable thing to do would be to say that Israel is a rogue state that is committing genocide, and exclude all Israeli companies.”

ICL Group, of which Norway holds a 1.65 percent shareholder stake, also contributes to the ethnic cleansing of Palestinian Bedouins in the Naqab Desert, as several mining projects are displacing them into small areas, according to Historians for Palestine. It also supplies fertilisers to illegal settlements.

Harlem warned that the portfolio may signal to financial market players that they “do not need to conduct thorough human rights and conflict-related due diligence regarding how their investments contribute to – or are linked to – war crimes and other serious violations of international law”.

Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Norway froze the fund’s investments in Russian companies.

Samandar called for the same treatment for Israel, which is similarly accused of war crimes.

The fund should not be a “passive observer of violations of international law,” he said. “It should be structured and managed so that Norwegian capital does not contribute to them.”

Norway recognised the Palestinian state in 2024 and backs a two-state solution.

A spokesperson at Norway’s finance ministry told Al Jazeera that “investments in areas affected by war and conflict require enhanced due diligence”, and that assessments of individual companies are made by Norges Bank and an ethics council “independently of the ministry”.

In January, Norway’s Palestine Committee filed a formal complaint, accusing Norges Bank, the fund and the authority that handles it, of serious crimes including genocide.

The case was dismissed, but the committee is appealing.

“If Norway expects other states and companies to respect international law, it must also ensure that Norwegian public money does not contribute to the occupation and oppression of Palestinians,” said Samandar.

articles.title: Merriam-Webster gives its dictionary a ‘glow-up’ with 1,400 new words and definitions
articles.summary: Merriam-Webster is giving its dictionary another “glow-up,” adding 1,400 words and definitions.
articles.body: Merriam-Webster is giving its dictionary another “glow-up,” adding 1,400 words and definitions. The dictionary publisher announced the additions on its website Tuesday. The new words and definitions include “shapewear,” “looksmaxxing” and “meme coin.” “The new entries reflect words and meanings that have demonstrated widespread use over time, offering a window into the world today,” it said in the release. Other words and definitions that made it into the dictionary include “parasocial,” “compute,” “vibe coding” and “superfood” (food rich in nutrients, including salmon, broccoli and blueberries). As temperatures drop across the country, Merriam-Webster fittingly added “cuffing season” to its dictionary. The company defines the term as “a time of the year when people who are not married or in a relationship begin looking for a short-term romantic partner to spend the colder months of the year with.” And amid widespread fears in recent days about AI’s impact on humanity, the company added “uncanny valley” to its collection of definitions. Merriam-Webster defines the term as “that creepy feeling that results from something artificial appearing almost—but not quite—human.” The nod to AI follows Merriam-Webster’s word of 2025, “slop,” which it defines as “digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence.” Merriam-Webster has not yet announced a Word of the Year for 2026. The company typically makes the announcement in the final quarter of the year. The company said on its website that it adds new words and phrases to its repertoire based on frequent, widespread and meaningful use. “The definer must judge whether there is enough evidence to put a new word in; that judgment will be reviewed by more senior colleagues as the dictionary moves through the editorial process, but there’s no committee, no advocacy, no meetings for new word inclusion,” the company said.
